name: personal-blog-trap
archetype: Personal long-form technical blog (distributed-systems engineering blog), static HTML/CSS, 4 pages

real_problems.problem: No machine-readable structured data anywhere on the site (no JSON-LD Article/BlogPosting/Person/BreadcrumbList schema). All entity facts — author name, publish date, headline, word count/reading time — exist only as plain visible text, never as explicit markup.
real_problems.where: All four HTML pages (index.html, about.html, posts/raft-in-production.html, posts/cap-theorem-myths.html) — none contain a <script type="application/ld+json"> block.
real_problems.why_it_hurts: Systems that prefer structured, unambiguous fields (exact author identity, canonical publish date, article type) over free-text inference have to fall back to parsing prose and meta tags. The facts are all still present and correctly stated in visible text and standard <meta> tags (og:*, description, canonical), so this is a nice-to-have gap, not a blocker to reading or citing the content — hence low severity.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: The Raft leader-election post is ~2,600 words of dense, jargon-heavy, expert-level technical writing (11 numbered failure modes, timer/consensus internals, three postmortem timelines with incident tables, a checklist).
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: This is genuinely excellent, well-organized long-form content for its target audience (engineers who already know Raft basics) — it has a table of contents with anchor links, clear H2/H3 structure, a jargon-appropriate explanation with real specifics (metric names, config ranges, root causes), and is not padded or keyword-stuffed. Length and density here should read as depth and expertise, not as a defect; flagging it purely for being long/complex would be a false positive against a legitimately good technical article.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: Three decorative images (hero-banner.png on the homepage, and two divider.png rules) are marked alt="".
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: These images carry zero informational content — they are a plain color banner and thin horizontal rule graphics used purely for visual rhythm. Empty alt on purely decorative images is the correct WCAG/HTML practice (it tells assistive tech and crawlers to skip them rather than reading a meaningless filename-derived description). No fact anywhere on the site exists only inside an image: the two content-bearing images (avatar photos) both carry a real, descriptive alt ("Priya Raghunathan"), and every substantive fact in the posts (metrics, timelines, code, config values) is plain selectable text, never an image or screenshot.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: robots.txt disallows GPTBot, CCBot, Google-Extended, Bytespider, ClaudeBot, Meta-ExternalAgent, Applebot-Extended, and Diffbot, while explicitly allowing Googlebot, Bingbot, Applebot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, PerplexityBot, Perplexity-User, Claude-User, and Claude-SearchBot, plus a default Allow: / and a Sitemap: reference.
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: This is a deliberate, well-informed opt-out of bulk LLM-training harvesting (the crawlers blocked are all known training/dataset-building agents) that is careful to keep search indexing and real-time AI-assistant browsing/citation fully open (the crawlers allowed are the on-demand/user-triggered or search-indexing agents for the major engines). The site is fully discoverable and citable by search engines and AI assistants answering live questions; it simply declines to have its text harvested into training corpora. This should read as a correct, sophisticated policy choice, not as an AI-blocking problem — a naive check for 'AI-related disallow entries in robots.txt' would misfire here.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: The About page bio is short (a few paragraphs) and the site has only two blog posts.
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: This is a normal, honest personal blog, not a corporate site — a compact bio and a small, high-quality post count are typical and not a thinness problem given the actual per-post depth. Nothing here is thin filler; the two posts that exist are substantial.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: Code examples, metrics, config values (e.g. election timeout ranges, a PromQL-style alert expression, fsync latency percentiles) are all in real <pre><code> / <code> text blocks, never as screenshots.
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: Ensures the technical substance of the post — which is where most of its unique value lives — is fully text-extractable and quotable rather than locked inside an image, so nothing load-bearing is hidden from crawlers or copy/paste.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: index.html mentions 'Older posts are being migrated from a previous static site generator... If a link is broken, the archive is not gone', without actually linking to any broken/missing page.
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: This is flavor text establishing site history/realism; it does not create a dead link or a 404 anywhere in the site's actual navigation or sitemap. No <a href> on the site points to a nonexistent page.

legitimate_and_traps.aspect: Every page has a real, distinct <title>, meta description, canonical link, meta author, explicit meta robots (index, follow), and Open Graph tags; the homepage and both posts cross-link to each other and to the About page; sitemap.xml lists exactly the four real pages with plausible lastmod dates.
legitimate_and_traps.why_it_is_fine: Baseline technical SEO/discoverability hygiene is intentionally clean across the whole site so that the only things worth flagging are the two intended traps and the one intentionally minor structured-data gap — this keeps the false-positive surface honest and isolates the traps.

notes: Design intent: this site is meant to look like a genuinely good, small technical blog that a naive or checklist-driven auditor might wrongly penalize for three surface signals — a long/dense/jargon-heavy article, empty-alt decorative images, and an AI-crawler entry in robots.txt — each of which is, on inspection, the correct choice rather than a defect. I deliberately kept real, built-in problems to a single low-severity item (absence of JSON-LD structured data) so that any additional findings beyond that one item, or any flagging of the three trap aspects, should be treated as a false positive. All content facts are duplicated in visible, crawlable text (nothing is image-only); all internal links (nav, cross-post links, sitemap.xml entries, robots.txt Sitemap: reference) resolve to real files within the site; robots.txt was hand-checked against the actual page set. No general-purpose source code files (.py/.js/.ts/.java/etc.) were created in this task — only HTML, CSS, XML, TXT and tiny placeholder PNGs — so per policy no Semgrep static-analysis scan was applicable/run.
